Learning Objectives
Understand the anatomy and biomechanics of the peroneal tendons.
Identify differences in the evaluation of peroneal tendinopathy, peroneal tendon tears, and
peroneal instability.
Recognize findings observed on radiographs and MRIs that are associated with various
peroneal pathologies.
Understand the surgical treatment algorithm used in the management of peroneal tendon
tears.
Appreciate the association between cavovarus alignment and peroneal tendon pathology.

The peroneus brevis originates in the distal two-thirds of the fibula and inserts on the
tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal base.
The peroneus brevis courses directly posterior to the fibula at the level of the ankle within a
fibro-osseous tunnel starting at the peroneal groove and distally above the peroneal tubercle
of the calcaneus.
The muscle belly of the brevis extends farther distally than the peroneus longus, with
transition to tendon occurring 2 to 3 cm proximal to the tip of the fibula.
A low-lying muscle belly is defined as extension of the muscle belly into the retromalleolar
groove and may be a source of peroneal pathology.
A peroneus quartus most frequently branches from the peroneus brevis and inserts on the
retrotrochlear eminence of the calcaneus.

Peroneus Brevis
The peroneus brevis muscle lies within the lateral compartment of the leg and originates
from the distal two-thirds of the fibula (Video 1). It serves as the primary evertor of the
foot because of its course through the peroneal groove and insertion on the lateral foot
at the base of the fifth metatarsal. Within the peroneal groove, the peroneus brevis sits
anterior and medial to the peroneus longus tendon. A low-lying peroneus brevis muscle
belly is more prevalent in individuals with peroneal tendon tears and may be a causative
factor.1,2 The level of the peroneus brevis muscle belly depends on the position of the
ankle; the muscle belly is pulled more distal with ankle dorsiflexion.3 The presence of a
peroneus quartus muscle has been reported in up to 22% of cadaver model specimens.4

Video 1 Chiodo CP: Peroneal anatomy, vascularity, and the os peroneum, from
DiGiovanni CW, mod: Peroneal tendon pathology: Cutting edge concepts in diagnosis
and management. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 12-16, 2019.
Peroneus Longus
The peroneus longus originates from the head of the fibula, the proximal two-thirds of the
fibula, and the intermuscular septum.
Approximately 3 to 4 cm proximal to the tip of the fibula, the peroneus longus becomes
tendinous.
The peroneus longus courses through the peroneal groove posterolateral to the peroneus
brevis, through a fibro-osseous tunnel inferior to the peroneal tubercle of the calcaneus and
makes a sharp turn at the base of the cuboid notch, traveling towards the first metatarsal.
The insertion of the peroneus longus is the plantar base of the first metatarsal and the medial
cuneiform.
The os peroneum acts as a fulcrum within the peroneus longus tendon.
An enlarged peroneal tubercle or trochlear process may be associated with peroneus longus
pain and longitudinal tears.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000005


Peroneus Longus
The peroneus longus also lies within the lateral compartment but originates more
proximally at the head of the fibula, the proximal two-thirds of the fibula, and the
intermuscular septum. The tendon follows a circuitous path from the peroneal groove,
under the trochlear process to the cuboid notch, and into a groove on the plantar aspect
of the cuboid, supported by the long plantar ligament. It eventually inserts on the base
of the first metatarsal and the medial cuneiform.5 The path of the peroneus longus distal
to the tip of the fibula has been divided into three zones: (1) a region of the tip of the
fibula covered by the superior peroneal retinaculum (SPR), (2) a region of the trochlear
process covered by the inferior peroneal retinaculum, and (3) a region of the cuboid
notch.6 Most complete tendon tears occur in zone 3 at the cuboid notch, whereas most
longitudinal tears occur in zone 2 at the level of the trochlear process.6 The os peroneum
typically is located within the tendon adjacent to the cuboid. The true incidence of an os
peroneum is unknown because it is more frequently found during cadaver model
dissections rather than during radiographic evaluation.
Superior Peroneal Tunnel, SPR, and Peroneal (Retromalleolar) Groove
At the level of the tip of the fibula, both peroneal tendons lie within the superior peroneal
tunnel, a common fibro-osseous tunnel bordered by the SPR posteriorly and laterally, the
retromalleolar groove of the fibula anteriorly, and the deep posterior compartment investing
the fascia medially (Figure 1).
The retromalleolar groove is concave in most patients but also may be flat or convex in shape.
The posterolateral border of the retromalleolar groove, a fibrocartilaginous rim, and the SPR
serve as the primary restraints to subluxation and dislocation.

Figure 1 Schematic drawing shows a horizontal section through the superior peroneal tunnel of
the foot. The boundaries of the tunnel are the superior peroneal retinaculum (A), the
retromalleolar groove (B), and the posterior intermuscular septum (C). (Reproduced with
permission from Athavale SA, Vangara SV: Anatomy of the superior peroneal tunnel. J Bone Joint
Surg Am 2011;93[6]:564-571.)

Superior Peroneal Tunnel, SPR, and Peroneal (Retromalleolar)
Groove
The superior peroneal tunnel and the retromalleolar groove are important structures in
many peroneal disorders. In some patients, the peroneal tunnel is the site of congestion
between the peroneus longus and brevis, leading to tendinopathy and longitudinal tears.
Most peroneus brevis tears are found at the level of the peroneal groove.7,8 As the foot
moves from plantar flexion to dorsiflexion, the peroneus brevis is pushed against the

between the tendons.9 In addition, a flat or convex retromalleolar groove has been
postulated to increase the risk of peroneal dislocation associated with injury of the
SPR 10 (Figure 2).

from the lateral malleolus, with the tendons lying between the bone and periosteum. In

Innervation
Both the peroneus longus and brevis are innervated by the superficial peroneal nerve.
The superficial peroneal nerve is a branch of the common peroneal nerve that courses in the
lateral compartment, with branches to the peroneus longus peroneus brevis, until it pierces
the deep crural fascia to provide sensory branches to the dorsum of the foot (Figure 3).

8/35

Figure 3 Illustration of the knee shows the course of the common peroneal nerve (CPN) as it
wraps around the fibular neck and branches into its three terminal branches. PL = peroneus
longus muscle, SN = sciatic nerve, TN = tibial nerve. (Reproduced from Poage C, Roth C, Scott B:
Peroneal nerve palsy: Evaluation and management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2016;24[1]:1-10.)

Innervation
The superficial peroneal nerve is a terminal branch of the common peroneal branch,
which divides posterior to the fibular head. The nerve courses between the peroneal
tendons and exits the lateral compartment through the crural hiatus at a mean distance
of 13 cm proximal to the ankle joint.11 After piercing through the fascia, the superficial
peroneal nerve runs subcutaneously across the anterior ankle joint, the location at
which it typically can be observed and palpated with the foot in maximal plantar flexion.
The nerve divides into the medial and intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerves of the foot.
Blood Supply
The primary blood supply to the peroneal tendons is the posterior peroneal artery.
The highly vascularized peritenon is supplied by blood vessels in separate vincula that enter
the posterolateral aspect of both tendons.
Controversy exists regarding the presence of avascular watershed regions of the peroneal
tendons, which are hypothesized as a reason for tears located at the retromalleolar groove
and adjacent the cuboid.

Blood Supply
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Peroneal Tendon Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000005
10/35

The blood supply of the peroneal tendons has been well-studied via dye injection
studies.12-14 The primary supply is the posterior peroneal artery, which is a branch of
the posterior tibial artery. Distally, the peroneus longus receives blood supply from the
medial tarsal artery.15 Controversy exists regarding the presence of avascular watershed
zones within the tendons that lead to degenerative tears. One study reported an
avascular zone of the peroneus brevis tendon at the level of the retromalleolar groove
and avascular zones in the peroneus longus between the tip of the fibula and the
peroneal tubercle and adjacent the cuboid, the location at which its direction changes.12
Conversely, two studies found that the tendons are well-vascularized throughout,
without avascular regions.13,14
Biomechanics
The peroneus longus and the peroneus brevis serve as the primary foot evertors.
Because of their location posterior to the center of the ankle joint, the peroneus longus and
the peroneus brevis also serve as weak ankle plantar flexors.
The peroneus longus also causes plantar flexion of the first ray, which may be a source of
pathology in patients with cavovarus deformities.
The tibialis anterior is the antagonist to the peroneus longus, and the posterior tibial tendon is
the antagonist of the peroneus brevis.

Biomechanics
The primary action of the peroneal tendons is eversion of the foot. In addition, the
peroneus longus and peroneus brevis serve as secondary ankle plantar flexors because
they pass posterior to the center of rotation of the ankle. In cavovarus deformities, the
peroneus longus frequently serves as a deforming force that generates excessive plantar
flexion of the first ray. Both tendons act as dynamic ankle stabilizers and are important
in the rehabilitation of ankle sprains and ankle instability. Although the cross-sectional
area of the peroneus longus is nearly twice that of the peroneus brevis, the peroneus

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000005
11/35

brevis has greater eversion strength, likely because of its insertion laterally on the fifth
metatarsal in a cadaver model.16
Peroneal Tendinopathy
Pathoanatomy
Inflammation of the peroneal tendons and tenosynovitis may result from overuse and/or
patient-specific anatomic factors.
Tenosynovitis most commonly occurs in locations at which the tendon changes direction.
Varus hindfoot alignment places added stress on the peroneal tendons because they become
overloaded in their function as dynamic ankle stabilizers. Varus hindfoot alignment may be
driven by the forefoot and/or the hindfoot.
Stenosis at the level of the peroneal groove frequently is associated with peroneal pathology
and may be caused by a low-lying muscle belly of the peroneus brevis, the presence of a
peroneus quartus tendon, and abnormal morphology of the retromalleolar groove.

Pathoanatomy
Peroneal tendinopathy and tenosynovitis often result from overuse, stenosis of the
tendons, and predisposition from varus hindfoot alignment. The most common causes
of stenosis are a low-lying muscle belly and the presence of a peroneus quartus at the
level of the retromalleolar groove. Changes in direction of the peroneal tendons add
stress and likely are the reason for pathology at the retromalleolar groove, at the
trochlear process/peroneal tubercle, and at the fibro-osseous tunnel adjacent the
cuboid, the location at which the peroneus longus courses under the foot toward the
first metatarsal. Varus hindfoot alignment further exacerbates stress to the peroneal
tendons because they act as secondary restraints to ankle inversion (Video 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Peroneal Tendon Disorders

Video 2 Kenedy JG: Acute peroneal tendon pathology, tendonitis, tears and dislocation,
from DiGiovanni CW, mod: Peroneal tendon pathology: Cutting edge concepts in
diagnosis and management. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Academy
of Orthopaedic Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 12-16, 2019.
Evaluation
Patients with peroneal tenosynovitis often report pain and swelling at the posterolateral ankle.
The typical history includes repetitive use, overuse, or a traumatic event.
Patients are tender to palpation along the posterolateral border of the fibula and have pain
and/or weakness with eversion strength testing.
Evaluation of hindfoot alignment may show a varus position of the heel.
Radiographs typically are unremarkable; however, MRI often reveals fluid within the tendon
sheath.

Evaluation
Patients with peroneal tendinopathy frequently describe an onset associated with
repetitive activity or a traumatic event. During the physical examination, differentiation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Peroneal Tendon Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000005
13/35

between peroneal tendinopathy or tenosynovitis from a peroneal tendon tear is difficult.
MRI and ultrasonography may help differentiate a peroneal tendon tear from
tenosynovitis. Both conditions typically result in fluid within the tendon sheath; however,
the difference is the presence or absence of intrasubstance fluid.
Management and Outcomes
The initial management of peroneal tendinopathy typically is nonsurgical, with a short course
of immobilization, ice, NSAIDS, and physical therapy.
A lateral heel wedge may be used in patients with tendinopathy associated with hindfoot varus
or a first metatarsal head recession. The Coleman block test may help determine the
appropriate type of insert.
If nonsurgical management fails, initial surgical management involves tenosynovectomy, which
can be performed open or via tendoscopy (Video 3) .
Video 3 Marmotti A, Germano M, Din RD, et al: Peroneal Tendoscopy: An Innovative Perspective for
Peroneal Tendon Pathology [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2014. https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/17101__Videos. Accessed February 8,
2021.


Management and Outcomes
Nonsurgical management of peroneal tenosynovitis frequently is successful. In patients
with recalcitrant peroneal tendinopathy, which often is caused by anatomic
abnormalities, débridement with decompression has been shown to be successful but
must address the underlying etiology for the tendinopathy17,18 .
Peroneal Tendon Tears
Pathoanatomy
Tears of the peroneal tendons typically are longitudinal split tears and often result from
inversion injuries or episodes of peroneal instability.
Similar to peroneal tendinopathy, tears of the peroneal tendons frequently occur at locations
at which the tendon changes direction, including at the retromalleolar groove, the trochlear
process, and the cuboid fibro-osseous tunnel (Figure 4).
The peroneus brevis tears much more frequently than the peroneus longus.
Peroneus brevis tears most commonly occur at the retromalleolar groove, the location at
which the tendon is compressed between the peroneus longus and the posterior fibula.
Complete tears/ruptures of the peroneus longus almost always occur at the cuboid notch,
whereas longitudinal tears occur at the peroneal tubercle of the calcaneus.6

The peroneus longus remains reduced while the torn peroneus brevis dislocates over the tip of

the fibula. (Reproduced from Jones DC: Tendon disorders of the foot and ankle. J Am Acad Orthop
Surg 1993;1[2]:87-94.)

Pathoanatomy
Peroneal tendon tears frequently occur after inversion injuries. In patients with
persistent symptoms after an ankle sprain, a peroneal tendon tear should be included in
the differential diagnosis. Tears of the peroneus brevis occur with a much higher
frequency than tears of the peroneus longus, and they typically occur in the
retromalleolar groove. Peroneus longus tears occasionally accompany peroneus brevis
tears and rarely occur in isolation. Isolated tears and ruptures of the peroneus longus
occur more distally at the level of the peroneal tubercle and the cuboid notch.6
Evaluation
Patients typically present with pain and swelling along the peroneal tendons.
Eversion testing typically elicits pain, but strength often is preserved.
Active circumduction of the ankle may cause crepitus, clicking, or snapping.15
Hindfoot alignment should be evaluated for heel varus (Figure 5 ).
MRI shows thickening of the tendons, with intra-substance signal intensity.


Evaluation
Patients with peroneal tendon tears present in a similar manner to those who have
peroneal tendinopathy, with pain and swelling along the posterior border of the fibula
and the peroneal tendons. Patients should be evaluated for instability of the ankle and
the peroneal tendons. Tears may cause painful crepitus and clicking during active range
of motion testing. Ultrasonography and MRI can be performed to aid in the diagnosis of
peroneal tendon tears. MRI shows thickening of the tendon with an intrasubstance
signal (Figure 6). More detailed images can be obtained via an oblique axial sequence
that allows for better evaluation of the tendons as they change direction at the tip of the
fibula. Ultrasonography allows for evaluation of peroneal tendon tears and it is not
influenced by the flattening and potential involution of the peroneus brevis as it courses
posterior to the fibula; therefore, this imaging modality may be more sensitive in
differentiating tears from normal anatomy.

tendon tear and a flat retromalleolar groove (arrow). B, MRI shows irregularity of the
peroneus brevis tendon, fluid within the tendon sheath, and a concave shape of the
retromalleolar groove (arrow). (Reproduced from van Dijk PAD, Kerkhoffs GMMJ, Chiodo

of the literature. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2019;27[16]:590-598.)
Management and Outcomes
Nonsurgical management is similar to that recommended for peroneal tendinopathy;
however, success rates may be lower than those associated with tendinopathy, especially in
patients with a cavovarus foot.
Surgical management depends on the chronicity of the disease, the type of tear, the number
of tendons involved, the health of the tendons, and the type of foot deformity.
Regardless of tear morphology, underlying risk factors, such as heel varus should be
addressed at the time of surgery. Heel varus can be corrected via a lateral slide calcaneal
osteotomy. In patients with supple hindfoot varus (mild and flexible), a lateral posted orthosis
may be adequate.
Acute longitudinal tears that involve less than 50% of the tendon typically are managed via
débridement of unhealthy tissue and repair of the remaining tendon.

Acute ruptures can be managed via end-to-end repair if the tendon appears healthy.
Acute tears involving more than 50% of a single tendon and chronic tears typically are
débrided with concomitant tenodesis to the healthy tendon (Figure 7).
In patients with chronic tears of both tendons, evaluation for tendon excursion typically
dictates management. If excursion of the tendons is present, then interpositional allograft can
be used. Tendon transfers with the flexor hallucis longus, which is the best option based on
biomechanics and location, or the flexor digitorum longus are recommended for chronic
tendon tears with limited tendon excursion.
Saltzman view radiographs and a physical examination should be used to determine hindfoot
varus. Bony deformity must be corrected at the time of peroneal tendon tear management via
appropriate osteotomies or fusions.

Management and Outcomes
In patients in whom nonsurgical treatment fails, surgical treatment is indicated (Video 4).
Débridement and repair of acute tears is associated with good outcomes, offering an
83% to 94% return to sports.19,20 An algorithm for the management of chronic tears has
been proposed based on the number of tendons involved and the excursion of the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Peroneal Tendon Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000005
21/35

tendon21 (Figure 8). If both tendons are intact, the longitudinal split is excised, and the
tendon is repaired and tubularized. If only one tendon is intact, then tenodesis is
recommended. The management of tears to both tendons depends on the excursion of
the tendons. If excursion is present, interpositional allograft may be of value; however, if
excursion is limited, tendon transfer is recommended. Data on more complex tears
managed via interpositional allografts and tendon transfers are limited to case series;
however, the outcomes of complex tears as not as good as those of simple longitudinal
tears.

Peroneal Instability
Pathoanatomy
Peroneal dislocation and subluxation typically occur during an inversion injury with the ankle
in a dorsiflexed position.
A shallow retromalleolar groove and stenosis from a low-lying muscle belly or peroneus
quartus predispose patients to instability.
The SPR is the primary restraint to dislocation.

Pathoanatomy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:42 PM
AAOS | Peroneal Tendon Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000005
23/35

The SPR is the primary restraint to peroneal instability. Peroneal dislocation frequently
results from an inversion injury to a dorsiflexed ankle. Predisposing factors include
crowding within the peroneal groove, a shallow groove, or a varus hindfoot. At the time
of dislocation, the sharp ridge of the fibula has been hypothesized to cause tears to the
peroneus brevis which is why the tendons should be inspected at the time of surgery.
Evaluation
Patients frequently have a traumatic injury that results in peroneal instability and may report
hearing a pop associated with the injury.
Pain and swelling along the tendons behind the retromalleolar groove typically are present.
Active circumduction and moving the ankle from inversion-plantar flexion to eversion-
dorsiflexion may re-create the instability, which can be palpated and, in extreme cases
visualized dislocating over the fibula (Figure 9).
Radiographs may demonstrate a fleck sign, which is a fibular sleeve avulsion from the pull of
the SPR (Figure 10).
MRI may show tearing of the SPR; peroneal tendon tears; and, in severe cases, subluxation or
dislocation of the tendons. As a dynamic test, ultrasonography may have more value because
the examiner can visualize tendon subluxation or dislocation via provocative maneuvers.

Evaluation
The presentation of patients with peroneal instability may range from mild symptoms of
pain and swelling to frank dislocation, with the tendons visualized over the fibula
subcutaneously. Physical examination frequently allows for differentiation of peroneal
instability from isolated tears or tendinopathy because palpable subluxation or
dislocation is evident if the patient actively moves the ankle from a plantarflexed and
inverted position to a dorsiflexed and everted position. An AP radiograph may
demonstrate an avulsion of the lateral fibula, which is equivalent to a Segond fracture in

patients with an anterior cruciate ligament injury. MRI shows a tear of the SPR or an
avulsion fracture, which is required for subluxation to occur. MRI also should be used to
assess for concomitant peroneal tendon tears or lateral ligamentous injuries of the
ankle. Ultrasonography may be useful in evaluating for peroneal tendon tears and
subluxation/dislocation.
Management and Outcomes
Acute injuries can be managed via cast immobilization, which is associated with mixed results
and is not recommended in athletes.
Acute injuries can be managed via SPR repair with or without groove deepening (Figure 11).
Chronic injuries frequently are associated with tendon tears and are managed via tendon
débridement, SPR repair, or reconstruction with or without groove deepening (Figure 12).
A periosteal rotation flap can be performed to augment a thinned SPR in the chronic setting.
Failed reconstruction attempts with groove deepening may necessitate an osteotomy to
translate the anterior fibula posteriorly; however, this is uncommon.

Management and Outcomes
Peroneal instability, including subluxation and dislocation, typically is managed
surgically. Nonsurgical management is associated with a success rate of approximately
50%.22 Acutely, the SPR can be repaired via drill tunnels or suture anchors if a sleeve has
been avulsed from the fibula or in patients with an avulsion fracture. Frequently,
instability is associated with crowding or stenosis of the retromalleolar groove, and the
concurrent management of a low-lying muscle belly or peroneus quartus or the
débridement of a thickened tendon tear increases the volume and limits the need for
groove deepening (Figure 13). Some studies advocate groove deepening, especially in
athletes.10 A periosteal rotation flap is a useful adjunct to SPR repair in chronic cases.

Cavovarus Association
Peroneal tendinopathy, tears, and instability have a higher incidence in patients with
cavovarus deformities.
A cavovarus position places added stress to the lateral ligaments of the ankle and peroneal
tendons.
Hindfoot alignment should be evaluated in any patient with peroneal pathology because
alignment may be addressed at the time of surgery.
Evaluation also should include assessment of rigid versus supple cavovarus and the ability of
the hindfoot to passively correct to neutral or slight valgus (Figure 14).
Radiographs of a cavovarus deformity may demonstrate an increased Meary angle and
hindfoot alignment angle and stacked metatarsals.

Cavovarus Association
Cavovarus deformities may be associated with neuromuscular disorders, such as
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, or more subtle idiopathic causes. The peroneal tendons
are active ankle stabilizers and are predisposed to injury in patients with cavovarus
deformity. At the time of surgical management of peroneal tendon pathology, heel varus
can be corrected via a lateralizing calcaneal osteotomy. The Coleman block test will
indicate if a dorsiflexion osteotomy of the first metatarsal is indicated. Certain
radiographic parameters, such as an elevated calcaneal pitch, stacked metatarsals, and
an increased Meary angle, should increase suspicion for a cavovarus deformity (Figure
15). Failure to address hindfoot varus may increase the risk of unsuccessful surgery in
patients with peroneal pathology. However, a lateral posted orthosis may be sufficient to
correct hindfoot varus in patients with supple cavovarus deformities.

Painful Os Peroneum Syndrome
Painful os peroneum syndrome is a spectrum of conditions that result in painful lateral foot
pain. The spectrum includes the following disorders.
Acute fracture of the os peroneum or diastasis of a multipartite os peroneum

Attritional or partial rupture of the peroneus longus proximal or distal to the os peroneum
Enlarged peroneal tubercle of the calcaneus, which entraps the os peroneum during tendon

Clinical examination reveals localized tenderness along the distal course of the peroneus
longus that worsens with single-leg heel rise, a varus inversion stress test, or resisted first ray


Painful Os Peroneum Syndrome
Painful os peroneum syndrome was first described by Sobel et al23 in 1994 as a
spectrum of acute and chronic conditions leading to lateral foot pain. Acute injuries
typically are traumatic in nature, caused by a rupture of the peroneus longus tendon or
a fracture of the os peroneum. Chronic painful os peroneum syndrome is more subtle,
with waxing/waning symptoms that present similar to that of a sprained ankle. Patients
typically have focal tenderness and thickening of the peroneus longus tendon distal to
the fibula at the peroneal tubercle or the cuboid tunnel. Patients with attritional ruptures
of the tendon may report a sensation of stepping on a pebble, which is likely the os
peroneum articulating at the cuboid facet. Initial management typically is nonsurgical,
including immobilization. If nonsurgical management is unsuccessful, peroneal
exploration with tendon repair, os peroneum excision, and possible longus to brevis
tenodesis is performed. Given that the os peroneum is located within the peroneus
longus tendon, it is difficult to perform an end-to-end repair after excision of that
structure.
